screens.title: Developing an Information Security Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter you'll learn how to craft an information security strategy that guides every security decision in your organization. A strategy is a long-term plan: it links a clear security vision to business objectives, assesses where you are today, defines a target security posture for the future, identifies gaps, and prioritizes initiatives in a roadmap. We'll work with familiar frameworks — NIST Cybersecurity Framework and ISO 27001 — to make those choices systematic and defensible. You'll also learn to separate strategic priorities from tactical projects and daily operational work, so your team can invest time and money where they deliver the greatest reduction in business risk. For example, a strategic objective might be to become a trusted provider of secure cloud services; a tactical response could be an 18-month migration plan; and an operational activity will be the Infrastructure as Code templates that enforce configuration. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to write a compact strategic statement, produce a gap-driven roadmap, select framework-informed objectives, and prepare the executive-level approval materials that secure buy-in and budget. Keep in mind that strategy explains why investments matter — not just what technologies to buy — and that executive support is required to make strategy real.

screens.title: Components of a Security Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: A complete information security strategy has specific components that together form a blueprint for action. Start with a vision and mission that describe the desired long-term security posture and how security supports business goals. The strategy must explicitly align to business objectives so security investments reduce business risk, not just technical risk. Next, document the current state using risk assessments, audits, and vulnerability scans; this baseline shows where you are now and what control effectiveness looks like. Define a future state — a target profile for the next three to five years — to articulate what success looks like. Perform a gap analysis to identify what is missing between current and future states. From the gap analysis, develop a roadmap: prioritized initiatives with timelines, resource estimates, and measurable outcomes. Also define governance: who approves the strategy, who owns initiatives, and how executive oversight will work. Finally, include metrics for success so the organization can measure progress and adjust the plan. For example, a metric could be percentage of critical assets with multi-factor authentication or time-to-detect for high-severity incidents. A common misconception is to list controls as a strategy; instead, strategy explains why controls are required and how they advance business goals. Your key takeaway is to always link each component to business impact and a measurable outcome.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Components of a Security Strategy
Core Concept

Components of a Security Strategy

Each component connects to business outcomes and ensures security decisions are prioritized and measurable.

Vision & Alignment
Statement of where security needs to be and how it supports business objectives.
Current & Target State
Baseline from assessments and a target profile for the 3–5 year horizon.
Gap Analysis & Roadmap
Identify initiatives, prioritize by business impact, and estimate timelines and resources.
Key Takeaway

Each strategy component must be tied to a measurable business outcome to guide investment and governance.

Roles & Governance

Define executive approval, owners for initiatives, steering committees, and review cadences so the strategy remains active and funded.

Metric Examples
  • % critical assets with MFA
  • Mean time to detect high-severity incidents
  • % of roadmap milestones completed on time
Common Mistake

Confusing a list of technologies with strategy. Strategy explains why those technologies are selected and how they reduce business risk.

Concrete Example

An objective might be: implement multi-factor authentication for all critical systems within 12 months to reduce account compromise risk and support enterprise client requirements.

Check Your Understanding

Ask: which metric will show the initiative reduced business risk, and who must sign the budget to fund it?

screens.title: Strategic Planning Process
screens.narratorSegment: Strategic planning in information security follows a repeatable sequence that ensures the strategy is grounded in business reality. Begin by understanding organizational context: mission, vision, values, and strategic business objectives. This clarifies what security must protect and why it matters. Next perform a current-state assessment using risk assessments, vulnerability scans, and audits to establish a baseline of controls, threats, and weaknesses. Then define a desired future state — the target security posture for a timeframe such as three to five years — balancing risk appetite and business priorities. Conduct a gap analysis that converts differences between the current and target states into actionable initiatives. Build a roadmap by prioritizing initiatives based on business impact and risk reduction; include timelines, resource estimates, and measurable success criteria. Finally, prepare approval materials and seek executive and board sign-off, establishing governance for delivery and review. A common misconception is to treat assessment outputs as the final product; instead, assessments inform prioritized initiatives. For example, a gap showing insufficient asset ownership might become a roadmap initiative to implement an asset inventory program. The process repeats as part of continuous improvement.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Strategic Planning Process
Process Flow

Strategic Planning Steps

1. Context
Map mission, vision, values, and business objectives that shape risk appetite.
2. Current State Assessment
Use risk assessments, audits, and scans to create a baseline of control effectiveness and threats.
3. Target State
Define the desired security posture over a 3–5 year horizon and set measurable targets.
4. Gap Analysis
Translate differences into initiatives and required investments.
5. Roadmap & Approval
Prioritize by business impact, produce executive materials, and secure governance and funding.
Concrete Example

If an assessment finds undocumented cloud assets, a strategic initiative could be: implement an enterprise asset inventory and ownership program within 12 months to reduce unknown-asset risk and support compliance efforts.

Supporting Points
  • Prioritization must be business-impact driven, not feature-driven.
  • Include measurable success criteria for each roadmap item.
  • Governance ensures initiatives receive ongoing executive attention.
Misconception
Treating an assessment report as strategy. Strategy requires prioritized initiatives and executive approval to allocate resources.

screens.title: NIST CSF vs ISO/IEC 27001
screens.narratorSegment: NIST CSF and ISO 27001 are two widely used frameworks that inform strategy in complementary ways. NIST CSF provides a flexible, risk-based approach centered on five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Use NIST when you want to map strategic objectives to an operational set of functions and when you need to translate risks into prioritized initiatives. For instance, a strategic objective under Identify could be to create a complete inventory of critical assets. ISO/IEC 27001, by contrast, provides requirements for establishing and operating an Information Security Management System. ISO 27001 is well-suited when the organization commits to a continuous management system — plan, do, check, act — and when certification or systematic auditability is a business goal. Both can be used together: use ISO 27001 to create a management system and NIST CSF to populate strategic objectives and measure function-level maturity. A common confusion is to assume they are mutually exclusive; instead, treat them as complementary tools. When preparing your strategy, state which framework anchors governance and which framework will guide specific initiatives so auditors and executives see a clear rationale.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › NIST CSF vs ISO/IEC 27001
NIST Cybersecurity Framework (CSF)
Flexible, function-based, risk-driven
  • Five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover.
  • Use to assess current vs target profiles and to generate prioritized initiatives.
  • Good for translating risks into concrete strategic objectives.
Example Strategic Objective

Develop a comprehensive inventory of critical information assets and assign owners to support risk-based prioritization.

ISO/IEC 27001
Management system standard for ISMS
  • Specifies requirements to establish, implement, maintain, and improve an ISMS.
  • Suited to organizations seeking a systematic, auditable approach and certifications.
  • Follows PDCA: Plan, Do, Check, Act for continual improvement.
Example Strategic Benefit

Use ISO 27001 as the governance anchor to demonstrate commitment and manage continuous improvement across initiatives.

Recommendation

Map ISO 27001 as the ISMS foundation and use NIST CSF to create measurable strategic objectives and maturity profiles. This dual approach ensures both governance and functional clarity.

screens.title: Strategic, Tactical, Operational Plans
screens.narratorSegment: Understanding the distinction between strategic, tactical, and operational plans is essential to prevent misalignment. A strategic plan is high-level and long-term: it states the organization's security vision and top objectives, such as becoming a leader in secure cloud services. Tactical plans break that strategy into measurable projects and shorter-term goals. For instance, a tactical plan might set a target to migrate 50% of on-premise applications to a secure cloud environment within 18 months. Tactical plans define what must be done and often include project scopes and milestones. Operational plans describe how to perform daily activities to deliver the tactics: runbooks, configuration templates, automation scripts, and monitoring procedures. An operational example would be implementing Infrastructure as Code templates to enforce cloud security configurations for each new deployment. A common mistake is to equate a list of operational controls with strategy; doing so creates fragmentation and reactive spending. The right relationship is hierarchical: strategy informs tactics, and tactics are executed by operations. To test alignment, trace each operational procedure back to a tactical objective and each tactical objective back to a strategic outcome.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Strategic, Tactical, Operational Plans
Definition

Strategy

High-level, multi-year goals that align security to business outcomes.

Tactics

Shorter-term projects and objectives that deliver strategic goals.

Operations

Day-to-day processes and procedures that implement tactics.

Example hierarchy
Strategic
Become a leader in secure cloud services over 3–5 years.
Tactical
Migrate 50% of applications to secure cloud within 18 months.
Operational
Create Infrastructure as Code templates to enforce cloud configurations per deployment.
Misconception

Treating tools and controls as strategy leads to fragmented investments and poor executive support.

Pro Tip

Trace each operational task back to a tactical milestone and each tactical milestone back to a strategic objective to validate alignment.

screens.title: Creating a 3–5 Year Roadmap
screens.narratorSegment: A strategic roadmap converts gaps into prioritized initiatives over a multi-year horizon, commonly three to five years. Start by listing all candidate initiatives from the gap analysis, then score each against business impact, risk reduction, cost, and feasibility. Prioritize initiatives by business impact and risk reduction — this prevents technical convenience from dictating investment. Assign target time windows and break initiatives into phases with measurable milestones. Include resource estimates and identify accountable owners for each initiative. For each roadmap item define success metrics, example: reduce time-to-detect for high-severity incidents by 40% within 24 months, or achieve 90% of critical assets with multi-factor authentication within 12 months. Keep the roadmap realistic: aim for a balanced pipeline of quick wins, medium-term projects, and longer transformational investments. Present the roadmap to executives with a clear ask: budget, people, and governance adjustments. A common mistake is to create a roadmap without metrics or owners — such roadmaps rarely get implemented. Ask yourself: which initiative delivers the most business impact in year one, and who must sign to fund it? Creating a 3–5 Year Roadmap means prioritize initiatives by business impact and risk reduction, include timelines, owners, resources, and measurable success criteria for each item.. In practical terms, prioritization, timelines, and measurable outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Creating a 3–5 Year Roadmap
Process

Roadmap: Prioritize and Plan

Quick Wins
Low-cost, high-impact items for year 1.
Medium Projects
18–36 month initiatives with measurable outcomes.
Transformational
Large, multi-year investments that change the security posture.
Measureable Example

Reduce mean time to detect high-severity incidents by 40% in 24 months; achieve 90% MFA on critical systems in 12 months.

Owner & Resources

Assign a senior owner, required FTE, and budget estimate for each initiative to enable approval discussions.

Common Mistake

Publishing a list without owners, timelines, or metrics; such items fail to attract resources and attention.

Roadmap Scoring
  1. Score business impact (high/med/low)
  2. Score risk reduction potential
  3. Estimate cost and feasibility
  4. Rank by combined score
Key Takeaway

A prioritized, measurable roadmap with owners and resources is the operational heart of a deliverable strategy.

screens.title: Governance and Roles
screens.narratorSegment: Governance is the mechanism that turns strategy into funded action. A governance structure spells out who approves the strategy, who owns initiatives, and how progress is reviewed. Common elements include an executive sponsor or board owner, a steering committee for prioritization, a program manager to track the roadmap, and accountable owners for each initiative. Define review cadences: quarterly steering meetings, monthly program updates, and annual strategy refresh. Governance should also specify decision thresholds for funding and risk acceptance. For example, small tactical projects may be approved by the security steering committee, while transformational investments require board approval. A common misconception is that governance is paperwork; in fact, it's the means to ensure initiatives receive resources and remain aligned to business priorities. Use clear RACI-style definitions so every initiative has an owner responsible for delivery, a sponsor who secures funding, consulted stakeholders, and informed parties. Clear roles reduce handoff delays and ensure the roadmap achieves measurable outcomes. Governance and Roles means define executive sponsors, steering committees, program managers, owners, review cadences, and decision thresholds to operationalize the strategy.. In practical terms, establishing approvals, ownership, and review cadences. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Governance and Roles
Process

Governance Components

Executive Sponsor / Board Owner
Provides strategic endorsement and secures funding commitments.
Steering Committee
Prioritizes roadmap items and resolves cross-functional trade-offs.
Program Manager & Owners
Tracks progress, assigns owners, and reports to governance bodies.
Cadences & Decisions
  • Quarterly steering committee for prioritization and funding decisions.
  • Monthly program updates for status and risk reporting.
  • Annual strategy refresh to adjust the target state and roadmap.
RACI Example

Each initiative should list: Responsible owner, Accountable sponsor, Consulted stakeholders, and Informed parties to avoid ambiguity.

Key Takeaway

Governance turns plans into funded action. Without definitions for approval and ownership, even the best roadmaps stall.

screens.title: Strategic Roadmap for CloudSecure Solutions
screens.narratorSegment: Let's take the CloudSecure Solutions scenario and propose one strategic initiative for each NIST CSF function. Under Identify, a strategic initiative could be to implement an enterprise asset management program to inventory all cloud resources, data, and application owners. This supports compliance and risk-driven prioritization. For Protect, the initiative might be to standardize and require multi-factor authentication for all critical systems to reduce account compromise risk and meet enterprise client expectations. For Detect, propose enhancing detection capability through a centralized logging and detection program with defined detection metrics and threat hunting cadence. Under Respond, a strategic initiative would be to formalize incident response playbooks, cross-team drills, and an escalation path that ties to business continuity objectives. For Recover, propose a program to test and strengthen backups and restoration procedures for critical services with defined recovery time objectives. Each initiative must include owners, metrics, and a timeline. A frequent mistake is to suggest tooling only; here, we emphasize programs with governance, metrics, and business-aligned outcomes. Hands-on Activity

CloudSecure Solutions: One Initiative per NIST Function

Identify

Initiative: Enterprise asset management program to inventory cloud resources and assign owners. Benefit: supports risk-based prioritization and compliance.

Protect

Initiative: Enforce multi-factor authentication for all critical systems with policy and monitoring. Benefit: reduces account compromise and aligns with enterprise client requirements.

Detect

Initiative: Centralized logging, detection engineering, and threat hunting program with detection SLAs. Benefit: faster identification of advanced threats and better incident context.

Respond

Initiative: Formal incident response playbooks, cross-team drills, and escalation paths tied to business objectives. Benefit: coordinated response and reduced business impact.

Recover

Initiative: Strengthen backup and restoration testing for critical services with defined recovery time objectives and regular exercises. Benefit: resilience and faster recovery after disruptions.

screens.title: Metrics and Continuous Improvement
screens.narratorSegment: Metrics are essential to show progress and justify continued investment. For each strategic initiative define clear success criteria and metrics tied to business outcomes. Examples from this chapter include percentage of critical assets protected by multi-factor authentication, mean time to detect high-severity incidents, and percentage of roadmap milestones completed on time. Use both outcome metrics and process metrics — outcome metrics show business impact, and process metrics show whether work is progressing as planned. Establish a reporting cadence within governance so metrics are reviewed at steering and board meetings. screens.title: Strategic vs Tactical Answer — Assessment Example
screens.narratorSegment: Assessments often include questions that test your ability to distinguish strategic initiatives from tactical and operational steps. Consider a finding that detection of advanced persistent threats is weak. A tactical response might be to deploy a new SIEM system; an operational activity could be training analysts on threat hunting or updating alert rules. A true strategic initiative, however, would involve developing a multi-year plan to enhance threat intelligence capabilities and integrate proactive detection across the enterprise with governance, budgets, and measurable maturity goals. The strategic initiative changes how the organization approaches detection at scale, not just which tool to deploy. When writing strategic answers, emphasize long-term scope, enterprise-wide integration, governance, and measurable reduction in business risk. A useful test is to ask: does this initiative require executive or board-level commitment and long-term funding? If yes, it is strategic. If not, it is likely tactical or operational. fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter you'll learn how to craft an information security strategy that guides every security decision in your organization. A strategy is a long-term plan: it links a clear security vision to business objectives, assesses where you are today, defines a target security posture for the future, identifies gaps, and prioritizes initiatives in a roadmap. We'll work with familiar frameworks — NIST Cybersecurity Framework and ISO 27001 — to make those choices systematic and defensible. You'll also learn to separate strategic priorities from tactical projects and daily operational work, so your team can invest time and money where they deliver the greatest reduction in business risk. For example, a strategic objective might be to become a trusted provider of secure cloud services; a tactical response could be an 18-month migration plan; and an operational activity will be the Infrastructure as Code templates that enforce configuration. By the end of the chapter you'll be able to write a compact strategic statement, produce a gap-driven roadmap, select framework-informed objectives, and prepare the executive-level approval materials that secure buy-in and budget. Keep in mind that strategy explains why investments matter — not just what technologies to buy — and that executive support is required to make strategy real.

These objectives will guide your work as a CISM when developing an information security strategy. First, you will be able to list and define the essential components of a strategy: vision, alignment to business goals, current and target state, gap analysis, roadmap, governance, roles, and metrics. Knowing these components helps you build a coherent document rather than a checklist of controls. Second, you will be able to describe the systematic process to develop, document, and obtain approval for a strategy. That process starts with context setting and assessment, moves to target definition and gap analysis, and ends with a prioritized roadmap and executive sign-off. Third, you will learn to use frameworks such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework and ISO 27001 to structure your strategy so it is auditable and repeatable. Finally, you will be able to differentiate strategic, tactical, and operational plans and explain their relationships, so plans at every level support the same objectives. Each objective includes a competency milestone to verify that you can convert assessments into prioritized initiatives and secure executive support.

These applied objectives show how you will use the strategy in practice. You will produce a current state assessment that uses risk findings, audits, and vulnerability scans to establish a baseline. This baseline enables a clear gap analysis when compared to the desired future state. You will then build a prioritized roadmap where initiatives are ranked by business impact and risk reduction rather than technical convenience. You will also prepare executive-level materials that explain why initiatives are required, estimate costs and timelines, and identify governance and roles for delivery. Finally, you will practice mapping NIST CSF functions to specific strategic objectives, for example, using Identify to create an asset inventory initiative and Protect to mandate multi-factor authentication for critical systems. These applied outcomes ensure you can move from analysis to a board-approved strategy and keep the strategy active through review and continuous improvement.

A complete information security strategy has specific components that together form a blueprint for action. Start with a vision and mission that describe the desired long-term security posture and how security supports business goals. The strategy must explicitly align to business objectives so security investments reduce business risk, not just technical risk. Next, document the current state using risk assessments, audits, and vulnerability scans; this baseline shows where you are now and what control effectiveness looks like. Define a future state — a target profile for the next three to five years — to articulate what success looks like. Perform a gap analysis to identify what is missing between current and future states. From the gap analysis, develop a roadmap: prioritized initiatives with timelines, resource estimates, and measurable outcomes. Also define governance: who approves the strategy, who owns initiatives, and how executive oversight will work. Finally, include metrics for success so the organization can measure progress and adjust the plan. For example, a metric could be percentage of critical assets with multi-factor authentication or time-to-detect for high-severity incidents. A common misconception is to list controls as a strategy; instead, strategy explains why controls are required and how they advance business goals. Your key takeaway is to always link each component to business impact and a measurable outcome.

Strategic planning in information security follows a repeatable sequence that ensures the strategy is grounded in business reality. Begin by understanding organizational context: mission, vision, values, and strategic business objectives. This clarifies what security must protect and why it matters. Next perform a current-state assessment using risk assessments, vulnerability scans, and audits to establish a baseline of controls, threats, and weaknesses. Then define a desired future state — the target security posture for a timeframe such as three to five years — balancing risk appetite and business priorities. Conduct a gap analysis that converts differences between the current and target states into actionable initiatives. Build a roadmap by prioritizing initiatives based on business impact and risk reduction; include timelines, resource estimates, and measurable success criteria. Finally, prepare approval materials and seek executive and board sign-off, establishing governance for delivery and review. A common misconception is to treat assessment outputs as the final product; instead, assessments inform prioritized initiatives. For example, a gap showing insufficient asset ownership might become a roadmap initiative to implement an asset inventory program. The process repeats as part of continuous improvement.

NIST CSF and ISO 27001 are two widely used frameworks that inform strategy in complementary ways. NIST CSF provides a flexible, risk-based approach centered on five core functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, and Recover. Use NIST when you want to map strategic objectives to an operational set of functions and when you need to translate risks into prioritized initiatives. For instance, a strategic objective under Identify could be to create a complete inventory of critical assets. ISO/IEC 27001, by contrast, provides requirements for establishing and operating an Information Security Management System. ISO 27001 is well-suited when the organization commits to a continuous management system — plan, do, check, act — and when certification or systematic auditability is a business goal. Both can be used together: use ISO 27001 to create a management system and NIST CSF to populate strategic objectives and measure function-level maturity. A common confusion is to assume they are mutually exclusive; instead, treat them as complementary tools. When preparing your strategy, state which framework anchors governance and which framework will guide specific initiatives so auditors and executives see a clear rationale.

Understanding the distinction between strategic, tactical, and operational plans is essential to prevent misalignment. A strategic plan is high-level and long-term: it states the organization's security vision and top objectives, such as becoming a leader in secure cloud services. Tactical plans break that strategy into measurable projects and shorter-term goals. For instance, a tactical plan might set a target to migrate 50% of on-premise applications to a secure cloud environment within 18 months. Tactical plans define what must be done and often include project scopes and milestones. Operational plans describe how to perform daily activities to deliver the tactics: runbooks, configuration templates, automation scripts, and monitoring procedures. An operational example would be implementing Infrastructure as Code templates to enforce cloud security configurations for each new deployment. A common mistake is to equate a list of operational controls with strategy; doing so creates fragmentation and reactive spending. The right relationship is hierarchical: strategy informs tactics, and tactics are executed by operations. To test alignment, trace each operational procedure back to a tactical objective and each tactical objective back to a strategic outcome.

A strategic roadmap converts gaps into prioritized initiatives over a multi-year horizon, commonly three to five years. Start by listing all candidate initiatives from the gap analysis, then score each against business impact, risk reduction, cost, and feasibility. Prioritize initiatives by business impact and risk reduction — this prevents technical convenience from dictating investment. Assign target time windows and break initiatives into phases with measurable milestones. Include resource estimates and identify accountable owners for each initiative. For each roadmap item define success metrics, example: reduce time-to-detect for high-severity incidents by 40% within 24 months, or achieve 90% of critical assets with multi-factor authentication within 12 months. Keep the roadmap realistic: aim for a balanced pipeline of quick wins, medium-term projects, and longer transformational investments. Present the roadmap to executives with a clear ask: budget, people, and governance adjustments. A common mistake is to create a roadmap without metrics or owners — such roadmaps rarely get implemented. Ask yourself: which initiative delivers the most business impact in year one, and who must sign to fund it? Creating a 3–5 Year Roadmap means prioritize initiatives by business impact and risk reduction, include timelines, owners, resources, and measurable success criteria for each item.. In practical terms, prioritization, timelines, and measurable outcomes. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Common elements include an executive sponsor or board owner, a steering committee for prioritization, a program manager to track the roadmap, and accountable owners for each initiative. Define review cadences: quarterly steering meetings, monthly program updates, and annual strategy refresh. Governance should also specify decision thresholds for funding and risk acceptance. For example, small tactical projects may be approved by the security steering committee, while transformational investments require board approval. Clear roles reduce handoff delays and ensure the roadmap achieves measurable outcomes. Let's summarize the most important concepts to carry forward. First, an information security strategy is a long-term, business-aligned plan that includes vision, current state, target state, gap analysis, a prioritized roadmap, governance, roles, and metrics. Second, the strategic planning process is repeatable: understand context, assess current state, define target state, perform gap analysis, build a prioritized roadmap, and secure approval and governance. Third, frameworks matter: use NIST CSF to map functions and objectives, and ISO 27001 to anchor governance with an auditable ISMS; the two are complementary. Fourth, clearly distinguish strategy from tactical and operational plans. Strategy sets direction and secures resources; tactics and operations implement that direction.
